en: The Kāṭhina-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya,
in one fascicle.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree during the Great Tang Dynasty.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then, a great number of bhikṣus, having completed their three-month rains retreat at Sāketa, each took up their robes and bowls and went to where the World-Honored One was.
Encountering mud and rain on the road, exhausted by the summer heat, with wild grasses cutting his body and sweat flowing all over him, he traveled by stages until he reached the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus set aside their robes and bowls, washed their feet, and approached the World-Honored One. They prostrated at his feet and sat to one side.
It was the World-Honored One’s constant custom, upon seeing visiting bhikṣus arrive, to greet them with mutual inquiry:
"From where have you come after completing your summer retreat?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Having completed our three-month rains retreat at Svāgata City, we have come here."
He asked, "While you were in retreat there during the three months of the rainy season, did you dwell in peace and comfort?
Was it not difficult for you to obtain food and drink through alms?"
He replied, "World-Honored One!
We have lived in peace and comfort for three months; food and drink were not difficult to obtain."
"We have come from there carrying our robes and bowls; along the road we traveled, we endured the hardships of mud and rain until our bodies were exhausted and weary as we gradually arrived here.
Having heard this, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"My disciples, having completed the summer retreat, are traveling through the human world carrying their robes and bowls; encountering mud and rain on the road, they have undergone extreme suffering and their physical forms are exhausted and weary."
I should now cause the bhikṣus to dwell in peace and happiness,
and for the sake of increasing the merit of all donors, I authorize the bhikṣus to spread the kaṭhina robe.
When spreading out this robe, there are five advantages:
first, there is no offense of exceeding ten days;
second, there is no offense of exceeding one month.
Third, there is no offense for being separated from one's robes overnight;
fourth, one may travel among human settlements wearing only the upper and lower robes;
fifth, one may, according to one's own wish, keep a surplus of robes.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of benefits:
first, obtaining food from a separate group;
second, obtaining food on multiple occasions.
Third, one may go to a layperson’s home to receive food even if not invited;
fourth, one may freely request as much clothing as desired;
fifth, from the middle of the eighth month until the middle of the first month, whatever wealth or goods are obtained during these five months constitute the benefits of the *kaṭhina* robe.
"When it is opened in this manner, it will cause all disciples to dwell in peace and happiness.
He then addressed the bhikṣus:

"In order to enable you to dwell in peace and happiness, and so that the merit of all donors may increase, the kaṭhina robe shall be spread for the community during the rainy season retreat; thereby, many benefits will be obtained, as in the ten previous cases."
"As the Blessed One has spoken of spreading the *kaṭhina* robe, the bhikṣus did not know how to spread it.
The Buddha said:

'During the three months of the rainy season retreat, when the community obtains robes and materials, they should be used to make robes. First, one should announce it with words to inform the assembly:'"
"Venerable Saṃgha, you should know that the community of bhikṣus who have completed the summer retreat has obtained this cloth.
If the Saṃgha so desires, let this material be used to make the kaṭhina robe for the community."
When the next day had arrived, the *gandī* was struck, the Saṃgha was assembled, and the formal announcement (*jñapti*) had been completed.
He then instructed a bhikṣu to make the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*), saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This robe is the property acquired by the Saṃgha during the rains retreat at this location; the Saṃgha now intends to make this robe into *kaṭhina*.
This robe shall be spread out as *kaṭhina* for the Saṃgha.
If the kaṭhina has already been spread, even if one goes outside the boundary, there is still no offense of being separated from one's three robes, let alone other garments.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now take this robe and have the bhikṣu so-and-so act as the kaṭhina-maker for the Saṃgha.
"If the robe has already been spread out, even if one goes outside the boundary, there is still no offense of being separated from the three robes, let alone other garments.
The motion (*jñapti*) is thus.
The formal ritual act (*karman*) is accomplished according to this motion.

Next, one must appoint a monk to spread the *kaṭhina* robe; he must possess five qualities and should be appointed after careful consideration. These are: being free from desire, hatred, malice, and delusion, and knowing when the *kaṭhina* has been spread and when it has not.
If it were otherwise, one should not appoint [the candidate].
Thus, the appointment should be made as a preliminary preparation (*pūrvaprayoga*).
Once the assembly has gathered, one should first ask whether they are capable or not, saying:
"O [Name]! Are you able to act as the robe-distributor for the Saṃgha?
If he says he is able, one should reply:
"I am able.
Then, a second bhikṣu performs the formal motion (jñapti-karman) and appoints him, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, wishes to serve as the person who spreads the kaṭhina robe; he shall now spread the kaṭhina for the Saṃgha.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha authorize this: the Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣu so-and-so to serve as the person who spreads the kaṭhina.
"This so-and-so shall spread the kaṭhina robe for the Saṃgha.
This is the formal announcement. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, desires to serve as the kaṭhina-spreaders; he now spreads the kaṭhina robe for the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha now appoints so-and-so to serve as the kaṭhina-spreader.
"Venerable sirs, this bhikṣu so-and-so shall spread the kaṭhina for the Saṃgha.
If you, venerable ones, consent to appoint so-and-so as the one who spreads the kaṭhina for the Saṃgha—let him who consents that so-and-so shall spread the kaṭhina for the Saṃgha remain silent;
he who does not consent, let him speak."

"The Saṃgha has already granted its consent that this person, so-and-so, shall act as the kaṭhina-spreader; this person, so-and-so, has now completed his service as the kaṭhina-spreader for the Saṃgha."
"The Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; I now hold it thus.
Thereafter, the monk who spreads the cloth should perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) and prepare the *kaṭhina* robe.
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This robe-cloth shall be made into a kaṭhina for the Saṃgha.
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has been appointed by the Saṃgha as the kaṭhina-spreader.”
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit this: the Saṃgha shall now make this robe into *kaṭhina* and entrust it to the bhikṣu [Name].
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
The formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) should be performed according to the announcement (*jñapti*).
Regarding the *kaṭhina* robe-making monk, his conduct is regulated as follows:
at the place where the robe is made, he must first wash, dye, cut, and sew it; even when sewing just two or three stitches together, he must do so in the presence of others.
Furthermore, one must repeatedly form this thought:
"This robe shall be spread as the kaṭhina for the Saṃgha; it is currently being spread as the kaṭhina; it has already been spread as the kaṭhina."
Regarding these three types of thoughts, it suffices to have the latter two; this also constitutes the performance of the ritual act.
If one does not do so, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
Next, on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the eighth month, the person in charge of affairs should inform the assembly, making the following formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable sirs!
Tomorrow I shall spread the kaṭhina robe for the community; may you each relinquish your old held robes and assemble at such-and-such a place."

The monk who spreads the robe shall arrange various named flowers upon it and perfume it with exquisite incense; he shall then strike the *gandī* to assemble the community, and the formal announcement shall be made three times.
One may take this robe and stand before the presiding elder (upādhyāya), holding the robe with both hands, and make the following formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This robe has been authorized by the Saṃgha to be spread as the *kaṭhina* robe. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have now been appointed by the Saṃgha to be the person who spreads the *kaṭhina*."
"I, [Name], am this kāṭhina-cloth; with this cloth, I shall spread it as the kāṭhina for the Saṃgha.
Thus he says three times.
Next, having spread out this robe, he stands before the Elder and speaks these words:
"Venerable Elder, please attend!
This robe has been authorized by the Saṃgha to serve as the kaṭhina robe; I, the bhikṣu [Name], am the one who shall extend this robe."
"I shall now spread this robe for the great assembly.
The Elder replied, "Excellent! Spread the robe!"
"Excellent, you have well spread the canopy!
Whatever wealth, profit, or benefit there is herein, I shall obtain it.
Thus he spoke three times, and even down to the very end of the procession, they all spoke these words.
“Excellent, O spreader of the cloth!
Most excellent, O spreader of the cloth!
Whatever wealth, profit, or benefit there may be herein, I shall obtain it.”

Next, one should further understand the rules for the keeper of the robe: one must not take this robe to the chamber for defecation or urination; one must not enter the kitchen or any place where there is smoke or fire; one must not leave it exposed in the open air; and one must not discard the robe outside the boundary.
If he goes out for a short time, he should not remain overnight.
If the monk who holds the robes does not act according to this rule, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
Once the month of the first summer retreat has arrived on the fifteenth day, the person holding the robes should make the following formal announcement (*jñapti*) before the assembly:
"Venerable ones, you should know!
Tomorrow the kaṭhina robe shall be taken out. Each of you should personally take charge of your own robes; as for any beneficial items, the assembly should divide them."
Upāli requested of the Blessed One, saying:
"How many kinds of persons are not qualified to spread out the robes?
The Buddha said:
“There are five kinds of persons:

namely, one who has not spent the rains retreat, one who has broken the rains retreat, one who has entered the rains retreat late, a novice (śrāmaṇera), and one who is absent at the time of the distribution of robes.”
Furthermore, there are five types of persons for whom the formal spreading of the robe (*kaṭhina-āstaraṇa*) is not valid:

namely, one who is undergoing the *parivāsa* penance; one who has completed the *parivāsa*; one who is undergoing the six-night penance (*ṣaḍrātra-carita*); one who has completed the six-night penance; and one who is under training (*śikṣamāṇā*).
“Venerable One!
How many kinds of people are there who obtain only material gain, yet derive no benefit?
The Buddha said:
“There are five kinds of persons:
namely, one who has not spent the rains, one who has broken the rains, one who has entered the rains late, a śrāmaṇera, and one who is not present before [the assembly].
Furthermore, there are another five kinds of persons:”

One who is practicing the parivāsa, one who has completed the parivāsa, one undergoing the six-night mānāpya, one who has completed the six-night mānāpya, and one who is under probation—these are said to receive benefits but provide no benefit.
“Venerable Sir!
How many kinds of people are there who possess neither benefit nor advantage?
The Buddha said:
"Upāli! There are five kinds of persons: namely, one who has been suspended for not seeing their offense;

one who has been suspended for committing a grave offense; one who has been suspended for not relinquishing wrong views; one who has spent the rains retreat elsewhere; and one who acts contrary to the Dharma and Vinaya after the Sangha has been split."
At that time, a large number of bhikṣus were traveling through the countryside when they encountered bandits who plundered them; they eventually arrived at the city of Śrāvastī.
Upon seeing them, the local bhikṣus asked, "Welcome, venerable ones!"
"Is your journey peaceful and secure?
He replied, "How could there be peace and security?"
"All these garments and requisites have been plundered by bandits.
He replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"Now we have a great abundance of robes here; if the *kaṭhina* robe is suspended, we may share and distribute them together with you, Venerable One.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If monks face circumstances involving bandits, they should suspend the *kaṭhina* robe."
One should emerge [from the robe] in this manner: having performed the preliminary rites as usual, one should have a bhikṣu perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
In this residence, the harmonious Saṃgha has together spread the kaṭhina robe."
Now there are many bhikṣus who, having been plundered by bandits, have arrived here without robes.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now extends the *kaṭhina* robe for these bhikṣus who were plundered by bandits.
"Thus it is announced.
The formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is completed according to this announcement, up until the conclusion of the binding.
Once the rite has been performed, all the beneficial goods are to be divided equally among those who receive the robes.
"Regarding the robes they have obtained, let each distribute them according to their own intention as gifts to those monks who were robbed and left without clothing.
Upāli then requested of the Blessed One,
"Venerable Sir!"

Regarding these various types of robes—thin and sparse robes, coarse robes, robes with many seams, robes made of ramie or hemp, robes with frayed edges, worn-out old robes, robes acquired through forfeiture, and shrouds from the dead—are they all suitable for use as *kaṭhina* robes?
The Buddha said,
"It is not appropriate.
[He asked,] "Venerable Sir!"

If the robe has been crushed by a stone mill; or if it belongs to another person; or if it is less than three or five cubits in size; or if it is not cut into patches; or if it is not pure; or if no one has been appointed as the robe-spreader; or if it is outside the boundary—may one spread such a robe?
The Buddha said, "It is not permissible. [The monk asked:
"If one obtains robes during the three months of the summer retreat, may they be made into a formal robe?"
The Buddha said, “It may.
[The monk asked: “If the three months of the summer retreat have concluded, may the robes obtained then be made into *kaṭhina* cloth?”
The Buddha said:
"It may be obtained.
If there are further numerous robes that are either legal or illegal, they should be understood according to the meaning of the preceding text.
Regarding the characteristics of the suspension of the *kaṭhina* robe, there are originally eight types.
What are these eight?
They are summarized in this verse:
First, the loss through the certainty of departure; second, the loss through the certainty of losing the robe;
third, the loss through hearing that one has departed while being outside the boundary; fourth, the loss through the severance of hope while departing with like-minded companions.
What is meant by "loss through the certainty of departure"?
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who, together with others in the same location, has received the kaṭhina robe.

Having finished making the robe, he feels no attachment to it and, taking up his bowl and robes, wishes to go to another region. If he goes beyond the boundary with the firm intention that he will not return, this is called "loss through definitive departure."
What is the indeterminate forfeiture?

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who, together with others in one place, has received the kaṭhina robe-cloth, but before having finished making the robe, he goes outside the boundary to seek cloth—whether he has not yet finished making it, or has already made half of it—and regarding this beneficial material and his dwelling place, he either feels attachment or lacks attachment, or he has expectations or lacks expectations, intending to return to make the robe or giving rise to doubts; this is called the indeterminate forfeiture.
What is the definitive loss?

For example, suppose there is a bhikṣu who, together with others in one place, has received the *kaṭhina* robe-cloth; before he has finished making the robe, he goes outside the boundary to seek cloth, thinking to himself:
"I shall return and make the robe."
Again, he thinks:
"I shall now go out and never return, nor will I be able to make a *cīvara*.
This is called "definitive loss."
What is the loss through misplacement?

It is as when a bhikṣu, together with others in one place, receives the *kaṭhina* robe; before the robe has been made, he goes outside the boundary to make a *cīvara*, begins the work of making it, and then loses that robe. This is called "loss through misplacement."
What is the fault of losing [the *kaṭhina*] through hearing?
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who, together with others in one place, has received the *kaṭhina* robe; before he has made the robe, he goes outside the boundary to seek cloth, thinking:
"Upon my return, I shall make the robe."
After he had departed, the assembly then proceeded to take out the *kaṭhina* robe.
Upon hearing that the *kaṭhina* robe was being taken out, he felt sympathetic joy in his heart, thinking:
"Excellent! The robe is being taken out."
This is called the forfeiture through being heard of [the robe].
What is the forfeiture through doubt regarding the boundary?
For example, there may be bhikṣus who, staying together in one place, have received the kaṭhina robe.
When a robe has not yet been made, a bhikṣu thinks to himself:
"I shall go beyond the boundary to make a cīvara;
whether it is finished or unfinished, whether I return or do not return."
When one has formed such a thought, the [robe] is lost upon leaving the boundary.
What is meant by "losing it through the severance of expectation"?

For example, suppose there is a bhikṣu who, together with others in the same place, receives the *kaṭhina* robe for making robes; before the making of the robes is finished, he leaves the boundary to search for materials, intending to return and make the robes.
Having arrived at that place, he seeks clothing but finds none; his hopes are severed. This is called "loss through severed hope.
What is "withdrawal by common consent"?

It is when, for example, there are bhikṣus staying together in one place who receive the *kaṭhina* robe and make it into a garment. They go outside the boundary to seek clothing, and later return to their residence to perform the formal act (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) with the assembly to withdraw the robe. This is called "withdrawal by common consent."
The Kāṭhina-vastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, in one fascicle.
